newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberians vote to draw line under long civil war.
newsitem.headline: Liberians vote to draw line under long civil war.

text.p: After seven years of devastating civil war, the people of Liberia vote on Saturday to elect a government for the first time in 12 years.
The presidential and general elections have special significance, coming soon before the 150th birthday on July 26 of the country founded by freed American slaves as Africa's first modern republic.

The polls wrap up a delicate peace process engineered by Liberia's West African neighbours, who have policed the faction-ridden country for seven years, disarming 60,000 guerrillas and guaranteeing the staging of elections.
"Africa is now on its feet walking ahead step by step," former Benin president Nicephore Soglo, one of more than 500 international poll observers in Liberia, said of the election.

All eyes are on former warlord Charles Taylor, who launched civil war in 1989. He rolled out a well-oiled electioneering machinery that put him in the forefront of 11 other rivals, according to many estimates.
Taylor has publicly apologised to Liberians for the agony caused by the war he started, and which has touched nearly every family in the land. More than 150,000 people have died.

Taylor's fanatical supporters say they have forgiven their candidate, whose appeal appears to be his charisma, backed by superior resources. He controlled the only nationwide radio station until donors established another to give rivals a fair hearing.

His toughest rival, according to Liberian analysts, is Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, a former minister, banker and senior U.N. official. The only woman in the presidential race, she projects an image of integrity and reconciliation.
She is not tainted by the war, and she says she has enough respectability abroad to help Liberia win badly needed foreign aid to rebuild a shattered infrastructure.
Western and African nations funding the elections are putting pressure on candidates -- among them three former warlords -- to accept the final result.

"We asked the political leaders if they will accept the result of the elections even if they lose and they have given us an affirmative answer," said former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, the most high-ranking poll monitor in Liberia.
Carter told a news conference the elections commission would release results regularly as they come in. Trouble could erupt if parties announce their own returns.
Voters are also electing 26 senators and 64 lower house deputies in the poll based on proportional representation.

Electoral officials said enthusiasm during voter registration pointed to a huge turnout. They said a total of 750,340 people registered in 15 days -- a high figure, given that half the pre-war population of 2.5 million has been displaced by the fighting.
Polls open at 7.00 A.M. (0700 GMT) and close at 4.00 P.M. (1600 GMT).
Early returns are expected from Sunday night with final results due around Wednesday night, electoral officials said.
